Tomato grows best in well-drained, fertile loamy soil rich in organic matter. It does not tolerate waterlogging, so avoid low fields where water stands, or plant on raised beds or ridges. Mix well-decomposed farmyard manure or compost into the soil while preparing the field, because organic matter improves drainage, water holding and nutrient supply for the whole season.

For tomato varieties, the basal dose is farmyard manure 25 tonnes per hectare, nitrogen 75 kg, phosphorus (P2O5) 100 kg and potassium (K2O) 50 kg per hectare, with borax 10 kg and zinc sulphate 50 kg per hectare. A top dressing of 75 kg nitrogen per hectare is given on the 30th day after planting or during earthing up. The total for the season is 150 kg nitrogen, 100 kg phosphorus and 50 kg potassium per hectare. Hybrids have a different recommendation.

Tomato needs steady soil moisture, especially during flowering and fruit development. Irregular watering, with dry spells followed by heavy watering, causes fruit cracking and blossom end rot. Drip irrigation and mulching help keep moisture even. Water at the base of the plant and avoid wetting the leaves, because wet leaves spread diseases such as early blight.

queries.q: What causes yellow leaves in tomato plants?
queries.answer: Yellow leaves on tomato plants can be caused by nitrogen deficiency, which makes older leaves pale yellow. Magnesium deficiency causes yellowing between the veins, while overwatering can lead to yellowing and root rot. Fungal diseases like early blight or Fusarium wilt also cause yellowing, and leaf curl virus makes leaves small and yellowish. It is also normal for the oldest leaves at the bottom to yellow as the plant ages.

Recommended Fertilizer Doses - Paddy fertilizer dose
For medium and long duration transplanted rice, the blanket recommendation is 150 kg nitrogen, 50 kg phosphorus (P2O5) and 50 kg potassium (K2O) per hectare. Nitrogen and potassium are applied in four equal splits, at basal, tillering, panicle initiation and heading stages, and all the phosphorus is applied as basal. Tillering and panicle initiation are crucial stages, so the quantity should not be reduced there.

Fertilizers and Plant Nutrients - How much fertilizer to use
The right fertilizer amount depends on the crop, the variety, the season and the nutrients already in the soil, so it should be based on a soil test. Use the recommendation on your Soil Health Card or from your local agriculture officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra. Using more fertilizer than recommended does not increase yield; it wastes money, can burn plants, encourages pests on soft growth, and pollutes soil and water.

Recommended Fertilizer Doses - Converting nutrients into fertilizer bags
Urea contains 46 percent nitrogen. DAP contains 18 percent nitrogen and 46 percent phosphorus (P2O5). Muriate of potash (MOP) contains 60 percent potassium (K2O). The phosphorus is usually given as DAP, whose nitrogen counts towards the nitrogen dose, and the remaining nitrogen is given as urea. The Smart Krishi screen does this calculation for the farmer's crop and area.

For irrigated ragi in Karnataka, the recommendation is 100 kg nitrogen, 50 kg phosphorus (P2O5) and 50 kg potassium (K2O) per hectare, with farmyard manure 7 to 12 tonnes per hectare. Half of the nitrogen and all the phosphorus and potassium are applied at sowing, and the remaining nitrogen is given in two equal splits after 30 and 50 days of sowing.

Tomato Leaf Problems - What to do about yellow leaves
First check the watering: if the soil is soggy, water less and improve drainage. If older leaves are evenly yellow and the plant is growing slowly, nitrogen may be short; follow your soil test recommendation for nitrogen. Remove and destroy leaves with blight spots, avoid wetting the leaves, and give space between plants for air flow, because blight spreads in wet, crowded conditions. Pull out and destroy plants with leaf curl virus or wilt so they do not spread to healthy plants, and control whiteflies. Rotate tomato with crops from a different family, because wilt and blight survive in the soil and crop residue. If you are not sure of the cause, show a sample of the affected plant to your local agriculture officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra.

Tomato Cultivation - Watering tomato
Tomato needs steady soil moisture, especially during flowering and fruit development. Irregular watering, with dry spells followed by heavy watering, causes fruit cracking and blossom end rot. Drip irrigation and mulching help keep moisture even. Water at the base of the plant and avoid wetting the leaves, because wet leaves spread diseases such as early blight.

Tomato Cultivation - Staking and care
Staking or trellising tomato plants keeps fruit and leaves off the soil, which reduces fruit rot and leaf disease and makes spraying and harvesting easier. Remove badly diseased lower leaves and keep the field free of weeds, which compete for water and nutrients and can harbour pests.

Tomato Leaf Problems - Why tomato leaves turn yellow
Yellow leaves on tomato have several possible causes, and the pattern of yellowing helps tell them apart. Nitrogen deficiency makes the older, lower leaves turn evenly pale yellow first, while new leaves stay green. Magnesium deficiency makes older leaves turn yellow between the veins while the veins stay green. Overwatering or waterlogging damages the roots, so leaves turn yellow and plants wilt even though the soil is wet. Early blight, a fungal disease, starts as brown spots with rings like a target on lower leaves, with yellow tissue around the spots. Fusarium wilt makes leaves yellow and wilt, often on one side of the plant first, and the inside of the stem turns brown. Tomato leaf curl virus makes leaves small, curled upward and yellowish, and plants stunted; it is spread by whiteflies. It is also normal for the oldest leaves at the very bottom to yellow slowly as the plant ages.

Rotate crops, and include legumes such as pulses, because legumes add nitrogen to the soil and rotation breaks pest and disease cycles. Keep the soil covered with a crop, cover crop or mulch, because bare soil loses moisture and topsoil to sun, wind and rain. Avoid burning crop residue, because burning destroys organic matter and soil organisms; incorporate or compost it instead. Avoid unnecessary deep ploughing and working wet soil, because these damage soil structure and cause compaction.

Soil Health - What healthy soil means
Healthy soil holds water and air, supplies nutrients to the crop, and is full of living organisms such as earthworms and microbes. Soil organic matter is the key: it feeds soil life, binds soil particles into crumbs, and helps the soil hold both water and nutrients.

Soil Health - Soil testing
A soil test shows the soil pH and the levels of nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Fertilizer and lime or gypsum recommendations should be based on a soil test, because applying nutrients the soil already has wastes money and can harm the soil and water. Farmers in India can get their soil tested and receive a Soil Health Card, which lists the nutrient status of the field and fertilizer recommendations for the crop.

Soil Health - Soil pH
Soil pH affects how well plants can take up nutrients. Acidic soils are usually corrected with agricultural lime, and alkaline or sodic soils with gypsum, but the type and amount must come from a soil test recommendation.

Recommended Fertilizer Doses - Ragi fertilizer dose
For irrigated ragi in Karnataka, the recommendation is 100 kg nitrogen, 50 kg phosphorus (P2O5) and 50 kg potassium (K2O) per hectare, with farmyard manure 7 to 12 tonnes per hectare. Half of the nitrogen and all the phosphorus and potassium are applied at sowing, and the remaining nitrogen is given in two equal splits after 30 and 50 days of sowing.

Recommended Fertilizer Doses - Converting nutrients into fertilizer bags
Urea contains 46 percent nitrogen. DAP contains 18 percent nitrogen and 46 percent phosphorus (P2O5). Muriate of potash (MOP) contains 60 percent potassium (K2O). The phosphorus is usually given as DAP, whose nitrogen counts towards the nitrogen dose, and the remaining nitrogen is given as urea. The Smart Krishi screen does this calculation for the farmer's crop and area.

Fertilizers and Plant Nutrients - How to apply fertilizer well
Apply phosphorus and potassium mostly at or before planting, because roots need them early. Give nitrogen in split doses over the season instead of all at once, because nitrogen is easily lost by washing away or into the air. Apply fertilizer to moist soil near the root zone and not touching stems or leaves, and water after applying, so nutrients reach the roots and do not burn the plant. Combine chemical fertilizers with organic manure, which is called integrated nutrient management, because organic matter helps the soil hold nutrients and improves long-term soil health.

Fertilizers and Plant Nutrients - Common fertilizers
Urea supplies nitrogen. DAP (diammonium phosphate) supplies phosphorus and some nitrogen. Muriate of potash (MOP) supplies potassium. NPK complex fertilizers supply all three in fixed proportions. Organic manures such as compost, farmyard manure and vermicompost supply small amounts of many nutrients and also improve the soil.

queries.answer_en: Yellow leaves on tomato can happen for many reasons. Nitrogen deficiency makes older leaves turn pale yellow, while magnesium deficiency turns leaves yellow between the veins. Overwatering can also cause yellowing and wilting because it damages the roots. Other causes include fungal diseases like early blight or viruses like leaf curl.
contexts:
Tomato Leaf Problems - Why tomato leaves turn yellow
Yellow leaves on tomato have several possible causes, and the pattern of yellowing helps tell them apart. Nitrogen deficiency makes the older, lower leaves turn evenly pale yellow first, while new leaves stay green. Magnesium deficiency makes older leaves turn yellow between the veins while the veins stay green. Overwatering or waterlogging damages the roots, so leaves turn yellow and plants wilt even though the soil is wet. Early blight, a fungal disease, starts as brown spots with rings like a target on lower leaves, with yellow tissue around the spots. Fusarium wilt makes leaves yellow and wilt, often on one side of the plant first, and the inside of the stem turns brown. Tomato leaf curl virus makes leaves small, curled upward and yellowish, and plants stunted; it is spread by whiteflies. It is also normal for the oldest leaves at the very bottom to yellow slowly as the plant ages.

Tomato Leaf Problems - What to do about yellow leaves
First check the watering: if the soil is soggy, water less and improve drainage. If older leaves are evenly yellow and the plant is growing slowly, nitrogen may be short; follow your soil test recommendation for nitrogen. Remove and destroy leaves with blight spots, avoid wetting the leaves, and give space between plants for air flow, because blight spreads in wet, crowded conditions. Pull out and destroy plants with leaf curl virus or wilt so they do not spread to healthy plants, and control whiteflies. Rotate tomato with crops from a different family, because wilt and blight survive in the soil and crop residue. If you are not sure of the cause, show a sample of the affected plant to your local agriculture officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra.

Soil Moisture and Irrigation - Signs of too little or too much water
Too little water: plants wilt in the afternoon and do not recover by evening, leaves curl or turn dull, and growth slows. Too much water: soil stays soggy, lower leaves turn yellow, roots may rot, and plants wilt even though the soil is wet.

Tomato Leaf Problems - Blossom end rot
Blossom end rot is a dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom end of the tomato fruit. It is caused by a lack of calcium reaching the developing fruit, which is most often due to uneven watering rather than a lack of calcium in the soil. Keeping soil moisture steady with regular watering and mulching is the main way to prevent it.

Soil Moisture and Irrigation - How to improve soil moisture
Mulch the soil with straw, dry leaves, crop residue or plastic mulch, because mulch shades the soil, reduces evaporation and keeps weeds down. Add organic matter such as compost or farmyard manure, because organic matter acts like a sponge and helps soil hold more water. Use drip irrigation where possible, because it delivers water slowly to the root zone with very little waste. Harvest rainwater with farm ponds, bunds and contour trenches, because they slow runoff and let more rain soak into the soil. Reduce unnecessary tillage, because each ploughing exposes moist soil to drying.

Soil Moisture Sensor Guide - What the soil moisture reading means
The Smart Krishi soil sensor reports soil moisture as a percentage. This percentage is a relative reading from the sensor, not a laboratory measurement, and the same number can mean different things in sandy soil and in clay soil. A higher number means wetter soil and a lower number means drier soil.

Soil Moisture and Irrigation - When to water crops
Water when the soil around the roots starts to dry, not on a fixed habit. Check the soil at root depth, not only the surface: take soil from a few centimetres down and press it in your hand. If it holds together and feels moist, the crop usually does not need water yet; if it is dry and crumbly, it is time to irrigate. The best time to water is early morning or evening, because less water is lost to evaporation and leaves dry before night, which reduces disease.

Soil Moisture and Irrigation - How to water
Watering deeply and less often is usually better than frequent light watering, because deep watering encourages deep roots that can find water during dry spells. Water at the base of the plant and avoid wetting the leaves, because wet leaves help fungal diseases spread. Avoid waterlogging, because roots need air; standing water damages roots and can cause yellow leaves and wilting. Water needs change with crop stage, soil type and weather: sandy soil dries faster than clay soil, and crops need more water in hot, windy weather.

For tomato varieties, the basal dose is farmyard manure 25 tonnes per hectare, nitrogen 75 kg, phosphorus (P2O5) 100 kg and potassium (K2O) 50 kg per hectare, with borax 10 kg and zinc sulphate 50 kg per hectare. A top dressing of 75 kg nitrogen per hectare is given on the 30th day after planting or during earthing up. The total for the season is 150 kg nitrogen, 100 kg phosphorus and 50 kg potassium per hectare. Hybrids have a different recommendation.

Tomato Cultivation - Fertilizer for tomato
Tomato needs nitrogen for leaf and vine growth, phosphorus for strong roots and flowering, and potassium for fruit size, colour and quality. Calcium is important for healthy fruit; a lack of calcium reaching the fruit causes blossom end rot. A common practice is to apply organic manure and the phosphorus and potassium at transplanting, and to give nitrogen in split doses during growth and fruiting. The general recommended dose is in the recommended fertilizer doses information; the exact quantities for your field depend on your soil test, so follow your Soil Health Card or the recommendation of your local agriculture officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra. Too much nitrogen gives lots of leaves but fewer fruits and makes plants softer and more attractive to pests.

Apply phosphorus and potassium mostly at or before planting, because roots need them early. Give nitrogen in split doses over the season instead of all at once, because nitrogen is easily lost by washing away or into the air. Combine chemical fertilizers with organic manure, which is called integrated nutrient management, because organic matter helps the soil hold nutrients and improves long-term soil health.

Fertilizers and Plant Nutrients - How much fertilizer to use
The right fertilizer amount depends on the crop, the variety, the season and the nutrients already in the soil, so it should be based on a soil test.
